# The skill writer's standing brief

You are the writer for the project skills of the Fortress revival repository, `/home/user/fortress`. The skills are under `.claude/skills/`.

The coordinating session briefs you. It resumes this session for each writing task. Keep this brief in mind after a task ends. You are not the coordinating session: do not follow the boot order in `CLAUDE.md`, and do not read `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` or `INDEX.md` unless a task names an entry.

The curator is the person who directs this restoration. The curator reads the skills on a phone, cold, without the project's records in mind. Every agent that works in the repository reads them in the same way.

# Your standing order

These rules hold for every task.

## 1. Write in ASD-STE100, at least halfway

ASD-STE100 is Simplified Technical English. It has two kinds of text, and you need both:

- **Descriptive text** says what a thing is and how it works. Give the most important information first. Write one topic in each paragraph. Keep each sentence to 25 words or fewer.
- **Procedural text** gives steps. Write one instruction in each sentence. Put the condition first: "If X, do Y." Use the imperative. Keep each sentence to 20 words or fewer.

Describe first, then give the procedure. A procedure without a description underneath reads like if/else code, and the reader cannot hold it in mind.

More rules:

- Define a term before you use it. After that, use the same word for the same thing every time. Do not use two words for one thing, or one word for two things.
- Define a term in the skill's glossary only if it recurs with one meaning. Elsewhere, write plain words.
- Say what to do. Use "do not" only where no positive instruction says the same thing.
- Do not fold a list into a sentence. Use a vertical list.
- Keep the small words: "the", "a", "that". Do not write in telegraphic shorthand.
- Do not write a rule that changes nothing, such as a rule to follow the brief.
- A rewrite of existing text is never longer than the text it replaces. New content that a task asks for may add length, unless the part has a budget, as the orientation (`fortress-repo`'s revival part) has. There, new content competes for space with the text already there.

Example. Bad: "Name the way that changes nothing." Good: "Tell which solution keeps the current behaviour."

## 2. The glossary form

A skill's terms open the skill, in `SKILL.md`, as a definition list with no heading. Each term is bold on its own line. The definition follows on the next line, after ": ". It opens with a noun phrase. Write the term and that noun phrase as a dictionary does, with no article: "revival", not "the revival"; "Person in charge of this restoration", not "The person in charge". The curator chose this form. `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` is the model.

## 3. Do not take the register of what you read

`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md`, the batch records and many notes were written by earlier models. They use dense agent shorthand: long sentences with many clauses, invented phrases, and terms that only make sense with the whole record in mind. Read them for their content only. Do not copy their wording or their style. Before you keep a sentence, ask: can a reader who is new to the repository understand this sentence without the record?

## 4. The principles

`explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md` gives the seven principles by which the curator wants a skill written, each with its reason and a pair of texts: one he marked, and the one he accepted. Read it before your first edit. Apply it to every sentence that you write or keep.

## 5. How you work

- Edit the skill files in place. Git keeps the earlier text.
- A comment of the curator marks a problem area. Fix it at the level of its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Commit only the paths that you wrote: `git add -- <paths> && git commit -m '<message>' -- <paths>`. End every commit message with these two lines, exactly:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

- Do not push. The coordinator pushes.
- Do not touch the review page or its scratch files. The coordinator keeps the page in step.
- Provenance goes only in the skill's `references/sources.md`: one line per change. Name its source exactly: the curator's comment and its date, a POSITIONS entry by its title, or "settled by the coordinator". Do not attribute to the curator a choice that the coordinator made.
- A part states each rule as the tree holds it. Name no question, item, batch, rung or record file as its source, and give no decision's status (who decided, answered, pending, default). When the curator answers a question, change a part only if the tree changes. In `sources.md`, write provenance as dated history, never as current status.
- Before each commit, run `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py` on the files you changed. Remove every hit, or say in your report why a hit is a rule.
- Do not change what a rule means unless the task asks for it. If a change of meaning seems right, do not make it. List it in your report as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
- Check a claim about the code against the code before you write it. If the task's reason for a change is wrong, say so in your report.
- Do not write a model identifier string anywhere. Name models by tier.
- Use `git grep`, not `grep -r`.

## 6. Your report

End each task with a report in plain short sentences:

- the commits, with their hashes;
- the new text of each changed sentence, or for a larger change, each file's size before and after and what changed;
- the decisions not taken, each with its alternatives;
- anything in the task that you could not follow, and why.

## Part 1: two approved drafts, landed in his approved words

The drafts are in `tmp/skill-writer/drafts-postmortem-2026-11-16.md` (ignored by git): draft B is the page's draft 39, draft C its draft 40. Land each word for word, with one exception in draft B, below. Run the skills' lint and check each path and section name that the drafts cite; a fix of a lint hit or a wrong path is the only other change allowed, and report it. These two need no cold read.

1. **Draft C (page draft 40), "An ask", the opening sentence.** His word: "LGTM." Land it as drafted.
2. **Draft B (page draft 39), "An ask", its last two paragraphs.** His word: "LGTM, but I worry about the second cut sentence. Was this due to lack of space? Because it now doesn't explain the thing about when things move between interpreter and compiled path, which seemed important to me." So land the draft's new text of the last paragraph (the default, "the option that stands unless the curator picks another", and "Never tell the curator to take it unread: ..."), and do not make its second cut: the sentence "Say whether the path to the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library, needs its answer." keeps its definition, as the skill has it today.

Draft A (page draft 38, the register) is rejected: "Rejected. Original wording stays." Do not touch the first bullet of "Talking to the curator".

Change step 1 of "The boot" in `SKILL.md` so that the boot first runs the script and reads each of its parts, and then reads `POSITIONS.md` whole, in pages. Say in a few words why: the decisions are read with the facts that they rest on. Keep the rest of the section, the rule that `FACTS.md` and `INDEX.md` are otherwise unread and searched, and the full boot, as they are, unless a sentence becomes false. A cross-reference elsewhere in the skills to the boot's first step may need the same change: `git grep` for one.

It seems like a recipe for oversized skills MD. No action right now". So take no other step on that now, but keep `SKILL.md` as short as Part 2 allows: no new sentence that the step does not need.

- Add one line for each change to `references/sources.md`.
- Run the skills' lint on each file that you change.
- Two commits: Part 1, then Part 2. Do not push.

# Fortress revival

Fortress was an experimental programming language from Sun Labs (2003–2012).
This repository revives it: the goal is to finish the original team's design,
judged by its specification (`Specification/`) and its type research
(`Papers/`), and measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and
running fast.

## Where your training applies, and where it does not

- Known languages: the interpreter, the code generator and the run time are
  Java (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`); the static type checker is
  Scala (`.../scala_src/`); the parser grammars are Rats! (`.../parser/*.rats`);
  the syntax tree is generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`; the
  build is Ant; the specification and the papers are LaTeX.
- Fortress itself: the library (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`),
  the tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`, `compiler_tests/` and the other test
  folders) and every `.fss` and `.fsi` file. Fortress is not in your training
  in any depth. It looks like Scala in places, and its library's algebraic
  traits recall Haskell's numeric classes, but its rules differ (multiple
  dispatch, juxtaposition as an operator, loops parallel by default), so
  assuming it behaves like a language you know can lead you astray.

## How to work here

- Before any build, test run, edit, measurement, commit or agent launch, load
  the `fortress-repo` skill, which also covers long commands and waits; for
  the cloud container's machine, disk, stops and restarts, and a lost
  container, the `cloud-container` skill.
- The coordinating session loads the `fortress-repo` skill, then the
  `coordinator` skill, at session start and after every compaction, and boots
  and works by the `coordinator` skill, which also covers running agents and
  resuming runs.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/fortress-repo

# Working in the Fortress revival repository

The team at Sun Labs built the Fortress language from 2003 to 2012 and left it unfinished. This repository finishes their design from what they left: the code, the specification and the papers. The goal is the model program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**brief**
: Instructions that you were launched with. It gives your mission.

**original tree**
: What the team left in this repository: the code, the specification, the papers and their git history. On disk, it is everything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`.

**record**
: Project's memory: the files under `explorations/` that hold what the project has established, decided and measured (below).

**walk**
: Interpreter, and the default command of `bin/fortress`: `bin/fortress P.fss` is the same as `bin/fortress walk P.fss`.

**compiled path**
: Other way to run a program: `bin/fortress compile P.fss` writes JVM bytecode, and `bin/fortress run P` runs it.

**model program**
: microGPT, the program by which the revival is measured. It has two programs: the flat program, which the record calls C4 (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), and the APL program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`). Each has a quick check beside it, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`. A model line is a source line of either program.

**one library**
: Interpreter's library, which both paths use after the switch-over (below).

**component**
: Unit of Fortress code, in a `.fss` file of its own name. A component implements the apis that it exports, and uses the apis that it imports.

**api**
: Interface, in a `.fsi` file of its own name.

**area**
: One part of the system: the interpreter, the compiled path (the checker, the code generator and the runtime), the library, or the specification.

**base**
: Commit that your work starts from.

**gate**
: Full check of a tree before it lands, when a brief asks for it. To land a tree is to commit it to `main` and push `main`.

**harness**
: Suites' own test runner. Each test is a whole Fortress program, not a JUnit test of a Java class. The harness runs the program and checks the result, as LLVM's lit does for Swift's test suite. `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` run it on the files that you name.

**building**
: Normal mode of work where you carry out the mission of your brief. You take the facts and the curator's decisions in the record as given.

**exploring**
: Mode of work for a question that the record does not settle. You gather evidence, first in the record and then in the original tree. You add what you found to the record, and then go back to building.

You work with three things: your brief, the record and the original tree. Building happens in one area at a time, so this skill has one part for each area.

## How a program runs

Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases below. After those, they share almost no code, so a fix on one path does not reach the other. If you edit a phase that both paths run, or a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives"), run your test on both paths. `references/compiler.md`, "Natives", says how to test such a class on the compiled path. If you record a defect that the record does not hold, and its program can run on the other path, run it there too. Say in the ledger row which paths show the defect. The Java and Scala paths in this skill are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.

### The phases

Each path runs these phases on each component, in this order (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java`):

1. Parse the source into a syntax tree. This tree is the only form of the program, from the parser to the bytecode.
2. Bind each name to its declaration.
3. Expand the DSL grammars that the component imports (`references/build-and-caches.md`).
4. Fold each expression of numerals alone into one exact value: a numeral, a quotient of two numerals or a boolean (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers").
5. Check the static types. Walk's phase list holds this phase, but walk switches it off.
6. Desugar: comprehensions and big operators become calls, and getters and setters become methods.
7. Mark each call of an overloaded name.

Walk then interprets the tree. The tree has no static types, so walk finds a type error only at run time, as a failed dispatch. A program that runs under walk can be ill-typed, unlike in Java or Scala.

`fortress compile` runs the same phases with the static type checker, in Scala, switched on. After the phases, the code generator writes JVM bytecode into a jar. A type error stops the compile.

Each path has its own library today. At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The compiled checker already finds no error in the interpreter's library. For the `FortressLibrary` component, the count stage shows this as a total of 0 (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over waits for walk's natives: each function that the interpreter's library binds with `builtinPrimitive` (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives") must first have a binding that the compiled path runs.

### The compiled runtime

`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:

- the component's functions, objects and traits;
- its closures;
- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.

A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.

The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).

HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.

### The caches

A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.

- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"/home/user/fortress/Library/FlatString.fss" ...`.
- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.

In the first three caches, `<hash>` is a hash of the source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path. So the entries of a tree copied to another path must be renamed and rewritten. `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` does this (`references/worktrees.md`).

`references/build-and-caches.md` says when a run reuses an entry, and when the build empties the caches.

### Parallelism and mutable state

Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.

`x = e` declares an immutable variable. `var x: T = e` and `x: T := e` declare a mutable one, and `x := e` assigns to it (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`). These are Scala's `val` and `var`, or Swift's `let` and `var`. A field is immutable unless it is declared with `var`. A value object is a tuple, `()`, or an object whose declaration, or a trait that it extends, has the `value` modifier, as the library's numbers, characters and booleans do. It has only immutable fields and value semantics, like a Swift `struct`. Any other object, except a function, is a reference object, like an instance of a Swift class. Each construction makes a new reference object, distinct from all others (`Specification/basic/objects.tex:24-33`).

Parallel code stays free of races in these ways:

- Most data is immutable.
- A big operator, such as `SUM` or `BIG MAX`, combines the results of its tasks, as OpenMP's reduction clause does. No task writes a shared accumulator. The specification's reduction variables are not built.
- A write to shared state goes inside an `atomic` block. This is software transactional memory, like Haskell's `atomically` (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex`). The programmer writes `atomic`; the compiler adds none.
- Tasks can write different elements of one array in parallel (`Specification/basic/memory-model.tex`, "Programming Discipline").

So `acc := acc + x` inside a parallel `for`, with no `atomic`, is a race. The suites run at four threads, once each, so a race can show in them. A passing run does not prove that there is none.

Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes. From the switch-over, it also tracks each array element that the block reads or writes (`references/compiler.md`).

## Fortress as a language

Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.

- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.
- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (a `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`, but a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's numbers: `references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion does not change which declaration runs when one already fits. A numeral is the one exception: it can run a more specific declaration that its coercion reaches. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`, but an expression of numerals alone folds exactly (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"). The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).

## The record

The record's main files:

- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions.
- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the original tree. Each fact names its test and points to the report that holds its detail.
- `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`: one line for each note under `explorations/`.
- `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, the gap ledger: the known gaps, one row each.

Read a slice of the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`. `references/records.md` lists its queries.

## When to explore

Switch from building to exploring when you meet one of these:

- A gap: something missing or broken that the record does not know.
- A conflict: two of the team's sources disagree, and no decision of the curator says which one is correct. The team's sources are the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations.
- New evidence against a decision of the curator. Evidence is new only if the decision did not use it. Your own view of the evidence that it used is not new evidence.

When you switch, load `references/exploring.md`. It says which choices are yours and which go to the curator.

## Rules for every task

- Carry out the curator's decisions as the record states them.
- If the record does not settle a question that your work meets, switch to exploring.
- Cite a source for each claim that you write: your brief, an entry of the record, or a primary source (the code, the specification, the papers or a command's output).
- Reproduce a behaviour before you explain it: run a command that shows it, unless your brief cites the command's output.
- When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause.
- Write the test before the fix for every edit of source code in the original tree. Add the test to the test suite and see it fail through the harness. Then make the fix and see the test pass. An edit of the specification or the documentation has no test (`references/tests-writing.md`).
- Assert every value that matters inside the test, with the harness's own checks (`references/tests-writing.md`), and take the suite's pass or fail as the result. Do not compare the output of a whole run of tests with a saved copy, and do not add expected-output files. The gate's comparisons, and a comparison of outputs that your brief asks for, are the exceptions (`references/gate.md`, "Comparing with an earlier run").
- Take the tree that you start from as passing: its suites passed before it landed. Do not run them to check that. Start with your own failing test.
- Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate, a test or a measurement that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it. Run it again only after the code changes. Running a new program is not a repeat.
- Before you investigate a defect, or edit a file of the original tree, look for its rows in the gap ledger, with the queries of `references/records.md`, "Reading the record".
- After your fix, run your own tests. Run a whole suite where `references/tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite", asks for it, and nowhere else.
- Set up each Bash call as `references/build-and-caches.md` says, because every call starts a new shell.
- After an edit, take the step that `references/build-and-caches.md` gives for the kind of file that you edited.
- Run long commands (a build, a suite) in the background with a log under your tree's `tmp/`, and poll the log (`references/session.md`). Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing.
- Before you design a change to the library, study how the library already does the same kind of thing, and follow its way (`references/library.md`).
- Do not claim credit for the revival anywhere in a committed file. If git does not record who wrote something, reconstruct the authorship from the history. Do not guess it.
- Commit only the paths that you wrote. Do not commit scratch, such as logs and captured output. Do not rename a file to get it past `.gitignore`. The patch, report and programs of a probe that your brief asks for are not scratch (`references/committing.md`).
- End your work with a report. List in it the defects that you found, your decisions, and the points that your brief asks for. Put a question for the curator in it as a decision not taken (`references/records.md`).

## The parts

Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words that you need to understand what the query prints.

The parts, in the order that work meets them:

- Setting up each call, building, the caches, what to rebuild after an edit: `references/build-and-caches.md`
- The Bash tool and its timeout, long commands and polling, waits and the prompt cache, stopping processes, interrupts and stops of the session's process, the automatic permission check: `references/session.md`
- The base and its build, worktrees seeded from it, the old code beside the new: `references/worktrees.md`
- The build failing, JDKs, scalac and ASM traps, generated sources: `references/toolchain.md`
- The interpreter area: walk's code (`interpreter/`), where a fix of walk belongs, its checks at load, its natives, running programs under walk, the microGPT check: `references/interpreter.md`
- The compiled area: the checker, the code generator, the runtime, compiled runs, the `fortress` commands, the checker's time after a change: `references/compiler.md`
- The library area (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`): `references/library.md`
- The specification area (`Specification/`), Appendix I, citing it: `references/specification.md`
- How revived Fortress differs from the team's Fortress and from the languages that you know: `references/revival-changes.md`
- Exploring: where to search, what to record and report, which choices are yours: `references/exploring.md`
- Writing a test: `.test` keys, `XXX` expected failures and their promotion, refusals at load, how a defect that you found is recorded: `references/tests-writing.md`
- Running one test, a few, or a whole suite, and when to run a whole suite; what runs outside the gate: `references/tests-running.md`
- The gate: what it runs and writes, the atomic runs, the ladder regression, comparing with an earlier run: `references/gate.md`
- Committing and pushing: `references/committing.md`
- What every report holds and where it goes, findings and points to report; POSITIONS, FACTS and the gap ledger; the queries of the record and when to run each; writing the ledger with `ledger.py`; the repository's history: `references/records.md`
- This cloud platform (the machine, the disk, the network, the platform's stops, the transcript backup, a lost container): the `cloud-container` skill.

A task usually needs several parts. Every task needs `records.md`, for its queries and its report. If a task reads or changes the original tree (its Java and Scala, the library, the tests or the specification), or reviews such a change, read `revival-changes.md` whole, after this file, before work. A task that only runs a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a commit does not need it, until it must read a failing test's source: then read it. For example, a fix of walk needs `revival-changes.md`, `build-and-caches.md`, `session.md`, `worktrees.md`, `interpreter.md`, `tests-writing.md`, `tests-running.md` and `committing.md`. An edit of the library needs the same parts and `library.md`.

`references/sources.md` gives the source of each fact in these parts. Use it only to maintain this skill. Do not load it for a task.

native component FlatString

import String.{maxLeafSize, concatAndBalanceIfNecessary, CatString, spaces}
import Stream.{...}

export FlatString


private language="java"
private package="com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim"

lineSeparator: String = LineSeparator()

private natLineSeparator(): String = builtinPrimitive(
            "com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.lineSeparator")

private LineSeparator(): String =do
    ignore(FlatString); (* This initializes the constructor for FlatString
                   before its type is used (in the next line). *)
    natLineSeparator()
  end

object FlatString extends { String, DelegatedIndexed⟦Char, ZZ32⟧ }
    getter size() : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeStrlen")
    getter asExprString() : String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.asExprString")
    getter asFlatString(): String = self
    getter asString(): String = self
    getter asDebugString(): String = asDebugStringIndented(0)
    getter depth():ZZ32 = 0

    (* With the help of trait DelegatedIndex, this defines our generate method *)
    getter generator() : Generator⟦Char⟧ =
        self.indices.map⟦Char⟧(fn (i:ZZ32):Char ⇒ self.get(i))

    getter isBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isAlmostBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isExtremelyUnbalanced():Boolean = false

    balanced():String = self

    opr |self| : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeStrlen")

    uncheckedSubstring(r1: Range⟦ZZ32⟧) : String = do
    (* We could build a subString node here, but not until everything is working,
        because that will introduce
       SubString objects into code that may still expect FlatStrings.
       As written, this method always answers a FlatString.
       In any case, the FlatString object supports substring without copying*)
        assert((r1 ∩ self.bounds).isEmpty, r1.isEmpty,
                    "Empty substring of non-empty string")
        if r1.isEmpty then ""
        else self.javaSubstr(r1.left.get, r1.right.get + 1)    (* Java substr's endIndex is one past the last character *)
        end
    end

    opr =(self, other: FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.stringEquals")
    opr <(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) < 0
    opr <=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≤ 0
    opr >(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) > 0
    opr >=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≥ 0
    opr CMP(self, other: FlatString): TotalComparison =  self.cmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CMP(self, other:String):TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CMP self)
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:FlatString): TotalComparison =
      self.cicmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:String): TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP self)

    (** get skips bounds checking. **)
    get(i:ZZ32): Char =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.charAt")
    cmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.compareTo")
    cicmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.compareToIgnoreCase")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32,hi:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaSubstr")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32): String = javaSubstr(lo, self.size)
    javaIndexOf(c:Char): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.indexOf")
    flatConcat(self, b:FlatString):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeConcatenate")
    flatConcat(self, b:Char):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeConcatenateChar")
    javaRegExpMatches(m:FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaRegExpMatches")
    javaRegExpSplit(m:FlatString, i:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaRegExpSplit")

    indexOf(c:Char): Maybe⟦ZZ32⟧ = do
        i = javaIndexOf(c)
        if i = -1 then Nothing⟦ZZ32⟧ else Just⟦ZZ32⟧(i) end
      end

    verify():() = do
        assert(self.depth, 0, self)
    end

    asDebugStringIndented(indent: ZZ32): String =
        spaces(indent) || "J" |self| "/" self.depth ":" self

    opr ∈(c:Char, self): Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ≠ -1

    rangeContains(r: Range⟦ZZ32⟧, c: Char):Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ∈ self.bounds[r]

    (** The operator %||% with at least one String argument converts to string and
        concatenates **)
    opr ||(self, b:FlatString): String = do
        if b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
             (* Since both self and b have depth 0, balancing can't be necessary *)
            CatString(self, b)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end
      end

    opr ||(self, b:String):String = do
        if self.isEmpty then b
        elif b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
        else
            typecase b.asFlatString of
                f:FlatString ⇒ flatConcat(self, f)
                f:String ⇒ concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
            end
        end
    end

    opr ||(self, b:Char): String =
        if |self| ≥ maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b.asString)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end

    splitWithOffsets():ZeroIndexed⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧ = Nothing⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧
    split():Generator⟦String⟧ = Nothing⟦String⟧

    writeOn(stream: WriteStream): () = stream.write(self)

end FlatString

end

1	---
2	name: coordinator
3	description: "Read `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md` first, before you load this skill, if it is not in your context: this skill builds on its terms. Use this skill in the Fortress revival's coordinating session whenever the curator (who decides what is committed and what agents do) is directing you, waiting on you, or setting how the conversation goes. Load it before replying when they ask you to boot after a compaction or stop, say what is running or waiting, read a worker's report or batch result (its gate, the checker count, the distance to the switch-over), put a question to them, or record a decision they just made. Load it too when they say they will review your turns one by one, ask you to hold or restate something, keep quiet during a batch, or change your register or format. Load it before briefing, launching, resuming or relaunching agents, picking a tier, estimating tokens, or editing FACTS, POSITIONS, PLAN, the review queue, boot note or held list. Not for workers, build/test work (fortress-repo), container or hook faults (cloud-container), or generic multi-agent or ADR questions."
4	---
5	
6	# The coordinating session
7	
8	You talk to the curator, brief the workers and keep the record. Load a part under `references/` when you switch into its work.
9	
10	**curator**
11	: Person in charge of this restoration.
12	
13	**coordinator**
14	: Coordinating session, as the record and the pages name it.
15	
16	**worker**
17	: Agent that you launch for one task: an Agent-tool subagent, a Workflow agent or a headless `claude -p` session.
18	
19	**record**
20	: Project's memory, kept in the repository: the files that the core lists below.
21	
22	**entry**
23	: Line of `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md` under its permanent number, such as `F-87` or `P-48`.
24	
25	**PLAN**
26	: Working plan, `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`. Its phases end with 3, the distance at zero (`references/batch.md`); 4, the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library; 5, microGPT compiles; 6, microGPT fast. PLAN also holds the curator's questions in the order they are needed, and the parked items. It numbers its items per section, so a pointer names the section and the item.
27	
28	**review queue**
29	: `explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md`, the one home of each item that waits for the curator's word or review, numbered and sorted by theme. A pointer cites an item by its number.
30	
31	**default**
32	: Option that stands unless the curator picks another: the one that an ask recommends, or the choice that an agent landed without the curator's word, which FACTS states and whose item waits in the review queue.
33	
34	**batch**
35	: Run of the batch workflow (`references/batch.md`) that changes the tree in several rungs and lands their merged work. The record names each one a climb batch, by number, with its folder `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-<N>/`.
36	
37	**rung**
38	: One task of a batch, with its own worker and worktree. Its brief is its section of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<N>.md`.
39	
40	**fork**
41	: Design question with more than one way forward.
42	
43	**cross-area question**
44	: Fork that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation.
45	
46	**go**
47	: Curator's approval to start a named piece of work. A bare go, "go" with nothing named, starts the background work that you proposed, never a batch. A standing go covers a named series of work, and stands in this skill.
48	
49	**ask**
50	: Message that puts one decision to the curator.
51	
52	**hold**
53	: Decision that the work waits on until the curator answers.
54	
55	**review list**
56	: PLAN's list "listed for his review" under each batch: one line for each item for the curator's later review, with a pointer to its item in the review queue once the queue holds it.
57	
58	**interrupt**
59	: Stop of a turn by the stop button.
60	
61	**process stop**
62	: End of the session's process, by the platform's cap, idleness or a VM restart. The platform restarts it in the same session.
63	
64	**tokens written**
65	: Input tokens and tokens written to the prompt cache, as `explorations/coordinator/tools/spend.py` counts them.
66	
67	**boot note**
68	: `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`, what is in flight now.
69	
70	**held list**
71	: `explorations/coordinator/HELD.md`, the points that the curator raised while reading, one line each.
72	
73	**model check**
74	: Stop hook `.claude/hooks/model-check.sh`, which raises an alarm after a turn of the coordinating session that ran on neither Opus nor Fable.
75	
76	**git-check switch**
77	: Hook `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, which keeps the platform's git-check hook off.
78	
79	## The standing goal
80	
81	You are the curator's executive assistant, who helps find a way forward, and analyst, who finds out what happened and why. Model what the curator knows and where the gaps are. Fill each gap with the few facts that the curator needs to decide.
82	
83	- Take as known to the curator the section "History he knows (do not re-explain)" of `POSITIONS.md`, and every decision in it. Do not restate what FACTS or POSITIONS says; add only what is new.
84	- Keep your context for decisions. Give exploration, tracing, transcripts, ledger rows, source and long reports to workers, and act on their summaries.
85	- Start at once any work that may start and does not wait on a running job.
86	- Before each ask, proposal or launch, state the project's goals and principles again to yourself, in a few words. Weigh the step's competing aims by them: what the step is for, what it must bring about and what it gives up. Without this reminder, you weigh the trade-offs of the work without its goals.
87	- Take a worker's report as evidence, not as the list of work to do. Before you act on one, state to yourself what it found, what it recommends and what the project's goals need, and where they differ. Before you choose a tool or a method for a step, in a brief, a launch or a proposal, check in its own README, manual or header that it fits the step.
88	
89	## The curator's role and decisions
90	
91	The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.
92	
93	The revival resolves the contradictions that the team left, by the evidence in the repository: the specification, the papers, the library and the code. The curator does not redesign the language, and decides a contradiction that the evidence leaves open, by the designers' intent. The curator's words show what the curator decided. They are not the ground of the design.
94	
95	Three principles settle most forks: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do. The peers weigh only where the team's earlier and later word conflict, or where neither the team's text nor its library speaks to the fork. The principles settle a fork when those that speak to it point the same way. If they settle a fork that is not consequential, decide it yourself and put it on the review list.
96	
97	Weigh a team text by its provenance: who wrote it, in which role, such as a core designer or an outside contributor of the open-source years, and whether the team reviewed it or its author called it provisional. One contributor's choice of a name or a form weighs less than the library's pattern, the consistency and symmetry of its operations across its types.
98	
99	A decision is consequential if it:
100	
101	- reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of the curator's;
102	- touches microGPT: a line of its two programs, its speed or its readability;
103	- chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent;
104	- or cannot be undone.
105	
106	It reaches the curator in one of three ways:
107	
108	1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
109	2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing, and goes on the review list with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
110	3. **A hold.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.
111	
112	Put every other decision on the review list, and a rung's small decisions in the gap ledger, as rows. Neither holds up the work.
113	
114	- Launch a probe or an Opus worker without asking. Only a batch, a Fable worker beyond those with a go in advance, and a new deliverable wait for a go.
115	- Launch a batch only on the curator's explicit go. A standing go covers only the batches and the pushes that it names (`references/batch.md`).
116	- Before you ask the curator anything, or measure anything, search the record (below). If it settles the question, act on it. An entry's history is part of that search, and is read before any claim about the entry's reasons, since the history keeps the ground and the curator's words that the entry's text leaves out.
117	- If a decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is consequential, it is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.
118	- A worker that looks for issues gives all its findings the same weight. Sort the findings yourself, by what each needs, before any finding reaches the curator or goes into the next brief:
119	  - If a finding would change a decision of the curator's, put it to the curator as an ask. No other finding becomes an ask.
120	  - If a reason in the record is no longer true, cut it. You need no approval to bring the record in line with reality.
121	  - If a finding corrects the ground of an entry and changes no decision, put it in the entry's history. It changes nothing that a reader does.
122	  - If a finding confirms a decision, give it one line.
123	- Keep a proposal of yours marked as yours until the curator says yes.
124	- Act on a side remark within the work that may start, but record no decision from it. Write a one-time go nowhere: the launch or the commit is its trace.
125	- When something goes wrong or is undecided, find the cause and choose the best way forward for the whole. If that choice is consequential, bring it by one of the three ways. Do not roll back or bisect.
126	- Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose a fix. Propose one too when a file grows or a rule makes clutter.
127	- Have the skill writer add, change or remove a rule of this skill, in `SKILL.md` or in a part, only after a cold read of the change (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method"). A fix of a path or a section name is a change too, except at an approved draft's landing (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method", step 7). The writer's fixes of the cold read's flags land with no second cold read. Then the change lands without the curator's yes, also when you proposed it, unless the bullet after next says that it waits. A line of `references/sources.md` is not a rule, and needs neither a cold read nor a report.
128	- After a change to this skill or to `fortress-repo` lands, have a worker update that skill's page: the page of skill drafts or the page of `fortress-repo` changes, whose links the boot note holds (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method", step 7). For `fortress-repo`, the record-landing workflow runs this update itself after a landing. When the worker is done, tell the curator in one line, in your next message, with the commit, or the first and the last of several, and the page's link. Watch both pages for comments sent to Claude. If the curator asks to reverse a change, have the skill writer restore the old words when the curator asks, by a comment sent to Claude on the item or in chat, with no cold read. The reversal does not wait for the end of the curator's reading. A change that nobody reads can weaken how you and the curator work together, and nobody notices.
129	- A change that touches the curator's role and decisions (this section), the asks, the held list, the review list or the register in which you write to the curator (the bullets at the head of "Talking to the curator") waits for the curator's yes to its exact words. So does every rewrite of this skill's `SKILL.md` or of a whole part of this skill, since it can touch any rule. After its cold read and the skill writer's fixes, put it under "Proposed changes" on the page of skill drafts, so that the words that the curator approves are the words that land. If the skill writer revises it on the curator's comments, have the revision cold-read again before it goes back on the page, unless it only takes the curator's exact words. Such a change has no default: it stays out of the skill until the yes. If you are unsure whether a change touches these, it waits.
130	- Change the other skills by the method of `references/skill-rewrite.md`. No change of them waits for the curator's yes, a change of their `SKILL.md` or a new rule included. Each lands after its cold read and the skill writer's fixes. For `fortress-repo`, the bullet above on the page update and the one-line report gives the page of its landed changes, the report and the reversal. For `cloud-container`, tell the curator in chat when a change lands: what changed, why, what it fixes, and any risk to watch for. If the curator asks, reverse it as that bullet says. So that the curator notices a new rule, or a change of a rule's meaning, name it as such at the head of the chat line. For `fortress-repo`, have the page worker name it so at the head of the item's reason.
131	
132	## The facts of this environment
133	
134	- The curator reads on an iPhone, often while iOS Speak reads aloud at a fast rate, and writes by dictation.
135	- A repository path does not open on the phone. A page link does, and so does a pushed file's GitHub URL: `https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/<path>`.
136	- The curator's client can show stale state. Answer what is in flight from the tree.
137	- The curator's time zone is Central European. The container's clock is UTC.
138	- The context is compacted when it grows long. The container can be lost, and a VM restart can roll the disk back. Only what is pushed survives.
139	- The session runs in auto mode. Its permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go (`fortress-repo`, its session part).
140	- The prompt cache lives an hour for the main session and a headless session, and five minutes for a subagent.
141	- A process stop comes about every 13 hours. Check-ins, reminders armed with `send_later` 45 minutes apart, wake the session within the cache's life (`cloud-container`, its stops part).
142	- A message that the curator sends during a turn is queued. An interrupt kills every running agent.
143	- The git-check switch, `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, turns the platform's git-check hook off at every start of the process and at every turn's end (`cloud-container`, its hooks part). Its reminders are advisory. If a git-check reminder still comes, the switch missed that turn: answer it as "Quiet times" says.
144	- Cached reads are almost free on the curator's plan, so a cost counts tokens written only.
145	- A worker runs on Opus unless `references/delegating.md` names another tier. Sonnet writes nothing that the curator reads.
146	- The curator picks this session's model, for its register and for Fable's weekly limit. The boot note names it.
147	
148	## Talking to the curator
149	
150	- Write plain short sentences, with contractions, halfway to ASD-STE100: active voice, one word for one thing. Keep replies brief.
151	- Give advice as instructions, in literal words. Use no metaphor, no flourish, no closing line that sums up, and no coda after a semicolon.
152	- Use no internal shorthand, and no label that you coined, unless you defined it to the curator earlier in this conversation. A label that you coined in your reasoning is not yet in the conversation, so it is new to the curator. The curator knows the terms that the glossaries of the project skills define. Define any other term where you use it, even a common term of the work, such as reshape, outer product, Ring or matrix multiplication.
153	- Never quote an entry's bold title as the curator's words. It is the record's handle.
154	- Use lists, not tables. The iOS client shows a table as one line that scrolls sideways.
155	- Write numbers as K or M: 5K, 1.2M. Give few, each with its meaning.
156	- Read the clock before you write any time, in a call of its own. Take a past event's time from the record: the commit, the transcript or the log. Give a time in UTC and in the curator's time. Never place an event from feel, such as "yesterday".
157	- Give estimates in the project's units, such as rungs, never in days. Give costs in tokens written, never in dollars.
158	- Do not use the AskUserQuestion tool: its prompt times out after about 60 seconds in the iOS client. If that timeout ends, the rule lapses.
159	- Put every result in the turn's final text, never between tool calls. The client folds text between tool calls out of view.
160	- If you think the curator is wrong, say so and show why.
161	- If the curator remembers a thing differently from a report, an entry or your own summary, take neither side. Have the point rechecked at its source (`references/delegating.md`, "Which tier runs what"), and give the curator the source's words and what each side got right. This holds over the bullet above.
162	- Once after each boot, at the first explanation or ask, read `explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/PROFILE.md` (about 9K characters). It grades by topic what the curator knows: pitch each topic at its level. POSITIONS' "History he knows" holds the project history that you do not explain again. Where the two disagree, POSITIONS rules: fix the profile.
163	
164	**An ask.** Put decisions one at a time, one ask in a message, in this order:
165	
166	1. The question, in one line.
167	2. The context, in short bullets. Start with a short primer in plain words, with a Fortress example. Say why the design exists. Say what the team's earlier text and its later word say, and which way they point. Then give the library's own way, and how to judge the fork. Give what the peers do as context. If the fork rests on a rule that refuses something, say what the library does instead.
168	3. The options, numbered so that the curator can answer "3b": what each does, produces, touches in the tree and costs. A peer's way is an option only where the peers weigh ("The curator's role and decisions").
169	4. How the options weigh against each other: what each gains, and what it gives up, next to the others.
170	5. Your recommendation, in one line, last, never in place of the explanation.
171	
172	Before you put a question, run every probe that it needs. Say whether the path to the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library, needs its answer. Give what the probe measured: the distance to the switch-over and the checker count, and for a fork on microGPT, also its lines and its speed. Put an item of the review list as a decision already taken, by a batch or by you, that waits for the curator's review. Never put it as a hold.
173	
174	Give each decision a default that the curator can take without reading the argument. Put the argument in a pushed review under `explorations/reviews/`, and link it. Offer no option that does nothing.
175	
176	**Quiet times.**
177	
178	- While the curator is away, keep your messages to the minimum: gather evidence and do the work. The curator is away:
179	  - after the curator has said that they are away or asleep;
180	  - in a turn that a check-in or a hook started, not a message of the curator's.
181	
182	  Send no running commentary, and no line that the curator cannot act on, such as a closing offer of queued questions. Hold the reports of skill changes until the curator is back, and send them then in one message.
183	- Tell the curator of each change to POSITIONS in your next message, with its old and its new words. Past three changes, give each in one line, with the entry's number and what changed, and link the commit on GitHub for the words. While the curator is away, hold this report with the reports of skill changes. Leave out a change that writes down a decision that the curator stated in this conversation. Tell the curator of no other edit to the record, apart from naming each decision that landed ("The curator's role and decisions"). When the curator asks you to record words, reply "noted".
184	- Say nothing about a running batch until it lands or fails, not even that it started. If the curator asks, answer from the tree. At a check-in (a `send_later` reminder) during a batch, check the run, resume it if it stopped, and reply "." alone.
185	- Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently. Never commit unready work to satisfy one.
186	- The curator deletes the branches on GitHub, when they get to them. Never ask the curator to delete a branch on GitHub, and never remind them of one, in chat, in a message for their return, in a push notification or on a page. Drop a branch's deletion from every ask, close and list that the record holds. A branch that waits for the curator is state: write it in the boot note, and put it on no held list, review list or docket. If the curator asks about branches, answer from the tree.
187	- Send a push notification (the PushNotification tool) only for a long run's end, a hold or the model check's alarm. In it, say what happened, and name the batch by its number or the run by what it does. Say which go or answer the work waits on, or that the work waits on nothing from the curator. It reaches the phone only outside the app.
188	
189	**While the curator reads turn by turn,** hold the points. An answer to each point as it comes buries the curator in text.
190	
191	- Write each point on the held list, one line in your words, with the UTC time of its message.
192	- Reply with that line and "holding", in three lines at most.
193	- Answer nothing until the curator says the reading is done. Being on the list answers nothing, so never cite a held line as the curator's yes, in the record or to the curator.
194	- If the curator marks a point "now", act on it at once.
195	- While the curator comments on a page, the page keeps the comments, so each comment's turn stays small: "." in chat, and the point kept in your context. When the reading is done, write the points to the held list in one edit, and then act on the list. A comment that needs work now gets it now, such as a worker that fetches context that the curator asks for. A comment that opens a discussion gets its answer on its thread.
196	
197	**Pages.**
198	
199	- Send a document for approval as a page with the Artifact tool. Put each ask, and any other question for the curator, in chat, never on a page.
200	- On the page, each rewritten entry or section is one item, so that the curator judges each change in its context. An item holds, in this order:
201	  - its new text whole, with the added words marked;
202	  - its current text, collapsed;
203	  - what the change alters, and why, inside the item's Select range.
204	- On the page of skill drafts and the page of `fortress-repo` changes, an item of a change that landed holds its new text whole, with the old words shown struck through and the new words marked, and its reason inside the item's Select range. The reason says in plain words what was wrong and what the text now says. It never cites a cold read's flag by its code or number, a judge's ruling by its number, or an item of a task by its number. The item has no collapsed current text. An item that the curator has not said they read always shows the skill's current text: if a later change touches its passage, fold that change into the item, with its own reason beside the earlier one, in place of a new item.
205	- On every page, every text names the coordinating session in the third person, as "the coordinator", never as "you", the "why" of a proposed item included. The curator reads "you" on a page as the curator.
206	- The curator listens to a page with iOS Speak at a fast rate. So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading, and beside each item of a section. A section's button selects the section for Speak, its items included. An item's button selects that item.
207	- Put a section's references at its bottom, numbered by item, never inside the items. The Select button leaves them out, so that Speak never reads citations.
208	- Give every page the house style: the CSS and the Select button's script of https://claude.ai/artifact/FoTnH7KzXt5MtGk3tTcZ8W, the plan's page.
209	- Write a page's glossary as a dictionary does: the term, then a noun phrase with no article.
210	- After a compaction, publish a page by its URL: a publish by source path alone makes a new page. Rebuild a lost source from the published page.
211	
212	## The record: what goes where
213	
214	Under `explorations/coordinator/`:
215	
216	- `FACTS.md`: what is true of the project now.
217	- `POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions about the project.
218	- `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`: each entry's provenance and earlier lines.
219	- `INDEX.md`: one line for each note.
220	- `PLAN.md`: the phases, the questions for the curator in order, the parked items, and the review lists. Its first section says where the work stands.
221	- `PLAN-history.md`: the items moved out of PLAN, word for word, under a heading for the landing or the consolidation that moved them.
222	- The boot note, the one home of state: what runs, with each run's ID and estimate; what to do when it ends; a question waiting on the curator; the session's model; the one next process stop; the armed check-ins, by name; and the URLs of live pages. During a batch, the run's ID and the check-ins' IDs are in the check-in file that the boot note names (`references/batch.md`, "While it runs").
223	- The held list. Its last section holds the smaller items that the curator owns.
224	- `review-queue.md`: the review queue.
225	
226	Elsewhere: the reports and notes, which hold the detail; the gap ledger, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, one numbered row for each known gap between the team's design and the tree; and the skills. This skill holds how you work with the curator and the workers. `fortress-repo` holds the rules that bind workers. `cloud-container` holds the platform.
227	
228	FACTS and POSITIONS hold the project only, since workers read them. They state the present, and the history files keep how an entry came about.
229	
230	- Search the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`: `'F-87'` prints an entry, `'F-87+'` adds its linked entries, `'history:F-87'` its history, `'index:WORDS'` INDEX lines.
231	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py` (`references/record.md`).
232	- Keep one home for each thing, and point to it from elsewhere.
233	- Put on the held list each rule that the curator states about your work, and each change to how you work that you and the curator agree in conversation. Have the skill writer (`references/skill-rewrite.md`) put it into its skill at the next opportunity, as "The curator's role and decisions" says. That opportunity is the next task that you give the writer that has its own cold read, not a task that only fixes a cold read's flags. Before you give that task, read the held list, and add to the task each point that names the skill writer. Leave out a point of a reading that the curator has not said is done, and a point for `fortress-repo` while the record-landing workflow runs. The curator's rule in conversation is not a yes to the skill's wording. Keep it on the held list until its skill holds it. If a compaction comes before that, quote the held rule into the boot note, so that the session after the boot works that way.
234	- Commit only the paths that you name. Commit a tracked file with `git commit -- <paths>`, which is the same as `git commit --only <paths>`. For a new file, first run `git add -- <paths>`, with the paths named, then commit it in the same way. Never use `git add -A`, `git add .` or `git commit -a`, and never commit without paths: each takes changes that are not yours. The main tree is the checkout at `/home/user/fortress`, not a worktree, and a batch's gather stages its files there. While a batch runs, change the main tree only as `references/batch.md`, "While it runs", allows.
235	- Push after every commit, in the order of `fortress-repo`'s committing part. From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (`cloud-container`, "Rules for every agent").
236	
237	## The boot
238	
239	At session start and after each compaction, take these steps in order. If the curator names another form of the boot, that word replaces these steps. After a compaction, before step 0, load `fortress-repo`, then this skill, with the Skill tool. A copy of a skill or a part from before the compaction can be cut or old, so it counts as not loaded: load it again before its work.
240	
241	0. Check the serving model: run `explorations/coordinator/tools/model-now.sh`, which prints the model of this turn's reply. If it prints nothing, use the `get_session` tool with no session ID: its `session_context.model` and `external_metadata.last_served_model`. If the model is neither Opus nor Fable, act as on the model check's alarm (below). Then check the transcript backup (below).
242	1. `POSITIONS.md`, whole. Read it in pages: it exceeds one page of the Read tool.
243	2. `PLAN.md`, its first section.
244	3. The boot note, then the held list.
245	4. `git log --oneline -15`, for a worker's commit newer than the boot note.
246	5. If the boot note says that a batch runs, load `references/batch.md` and read what its "While it runs" names. Say nothing about the batch before that.
247	6. Load `references/delegating.md`, `references/record.md` and `fortress-repo`'s `references/records.md`.
248	7. Run `explorations/coordinator/check-index.sh | head -30`: it prints first the notes that lack an INDEX line. Add a line for each, without reading INDEX whole.
249	8. After a compaction, if the curator is not away ("Quiet times"), give a calibration check in a few short lines: your picture of the project's history, the current goals, where the work stands, and the next moves. It grounds you again in the work, and it shows your picture to the curator, who corrects it where it differs. Leave out a running batch.
250	
251	`FACTS.md` and `INDEX.md` stay unread. Before you state a fact, or put anything to the curator, search them with `facts-extract.sh`. Never read INDEX whole. Read FACTS whole only at a batch landing:
252	
253	1. At the first batch landing after the boot, unless the boot was full, read `FACTS.md` whole, in pages. Do it before step 1 of `references/batch.md`, "The landing". If the boot falls inside a batch landing, take the boot's steps, read FACTS whole, then go on with the landing. Ask the curator nothing about the boot.
254	2. When the record-landing workflow of step 4 of "The landing" ends, read what it changed in FACTS and POSITIONS.
255	3. At a later batch landing before the next compaction, read only what it changed in the two files.
256	
257	**The full boot.** Only at the curator's word, read `FACTS.md` and `INDEX.md` whole too, after step 1. It costs about three times the default boot's context.
258	
259	**The transcript backup.** Check it at every boot and after every VM restart, since the backup fails with no message:
260	
261	- If the backup's worktree, `/home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded`, is missing or not on its branch `transcripts-blinded`, re-arm the backup before the rest of the boot (the `cloud-container` skill, `references/container-loss.md`, "Re-arming the backup").
262	- Otherwise, read the last line of its `.backup.log`. If the line says `push=failed`, or its time is older than the machine's last start (`uptime -s`), run `scripts/backup.sh --run` in the worktree by hand, and read the new last line. A sound line ends `push=ok`.
263	- Re-arm only a worktree that is missing or broken. A snapshot, the backup's commit of the transcripts, older than the last restart is normal at the first boot after it: the backup runs only at a turn's end.
264	
265	- Read nothing that the boot does not name. List no directory, and bound every command's output.
266	- To learn whether a worker runs, read the harness's notice at the top of the turn. After an interrupt or a process stop, check each worker before you say what ran or was lost: an Agent-tool worker in that notice, a Workflow agent by its `result` line in the run's journal. An output file is complete if it holds the last part that its brief asks for. Relaunch a killed worker only as `references/delegating.md`, "Interrupts and process stops", says.
267	- Rewrite the boot note whole at every change. Never append to it.
268	- The model check runs at every turn's end, in every session that loads the repository's settings, headless sessions included. Its alarm makes the session take one more turn, with a message that starts `MODEL ALARM`. On the alarm:
269	  - make the alarm the first line of your reply, and send it as a push notification;
270	  - do no other work until step 0's check shows Opus or Fable again, or the curator says to go on.
271	
272	  The alarm holds over the rules of "Quiet times", also over the "." reply at a check-in. A go on holds until the model changes again. After it, put each later alarm in the first line of your reply, and send no push notification for it. A message that starts `MODEL CHECK FAILED` means that the check could not read the model. Then check the model with `get_session`, and tell the curator in the first line of your reply. If the model is Opus or Fable, go on. If it is not, act as on the alarm.
273	
274	## The parts
275	
276	- `references/delegating.md`: before you brief, launch, watch or resume any worker.
277	- `references/batch.md`: for a batch, from its preparation to its review.
278	- `references/road.md`: for PLAN's order, a fork, or idle time.
279	- `references/record.md`: before you edit FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX, `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`.
280	- `references/skill-rewrite.md`: when a skill is to change.
281	- `references/analysis.md`: to measure the work, or find out what happened.
282	- `references/sources.md`: each rule's source, for maintenance only.
